newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban makes tentative foray into Panjsher valley.
newsitem.headline: Taleban makes tentative foray into Panjsher valley.

text.p: Taleban-controlled Kabul Radio said on Wednesday that Taleban forces had entered the Panjsher Valley, the stronghold of former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.
It said the Taleban had made some gains during its advance late on Tuesday, but gave no more details.
There was no word on casualties.
The radio said the front-line near the Salang tunnel between Taleban forces and those of northern Uzbek militia leader general Abdul Rashid Dostum was quiet.
"There was no provocation in Salang between Dostum and Taleban," the radio.

The Taleban on Tuesday disowned an ultimatum sent by a Taleban commander to Dostum's forces the previous day that told Dostum to stand aside and let the Taleban cross the Salang pass over the formidable Hindu Kush mountain range.
Taleban Acting Deputy Foreign Minister Sher Mohammed Stanakzai told reporters on Tuesday that the ultimatum was unauthorised and not valid.
"Whoever handed over that letter was an enemy to us and Dostum," Stanakzai said.

A Taleban commander at the Salang front, Mullah Ghulam Mohammad, told a visiting United Nations official in the presence of reporters on Monday that he had asked Dostum's forces to stand aside because the former communist general "does not represent the people of the north," but said Dostum appeared bent on confrontation.
Stanakzai said the Taleban had decided to drive Masood's forces out of the Panjsher Valley, but had no quarrels with Dostum.
Masood withdrew to his Panjsher heartland base when Kabul fell to the Taleban with hardly a shot being fired.
"So far, we have no problem with Dostum, and we hope this will be solved through negotiations. We don't want more fighting," Stanakzai said. "We hope for a mutual understanding with Dostum."
Officials with Dostum's well-armed Jumbish-i-Milli faction have said they would fight if the Taleban pushed further north.
The Taleban appear to be keen to avoid a confrontation with Dostum at least until they have dealt with what they perceive as a threat from Masood's depleted forces.
Stanakzai said Masood had large dumps of arms and ammunition in the Panjsher Valley that represented a "strategic danger".
"We have to clear Masood's forces from the Panjsher," he said. "We hope it will be done very soon."
The Taleban on Tuesday issued a surrender-or-else ultimatum to Masood.
The Taleban came into confrontation with Dostum for the first time on Tuesday after capturing Jabal os-Siraj, a Masood stronghold 70 km (45 miles) north of Kabul.
Military experts said on Tuesday that Masood and Dostum may have to bury an old rivalry to confront the Taleban.
Dostum, once defence minister in Rabbani's government, was involved in an attempt to seize Kabul in a military coup on January 1, 1994, setting off bloody fighting with Masood forces.
Aides to Masood at a secret location in the Panjsher Valley said on Tuesday that some contacts were continuing with Dostum, but indicated that the two men were far from reaching an agreement.

U.N. Special Envoy to Afghanistan Norbert Holl was due to meet Dostum in the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif on Wednesday before flying to Kabul for talks with Taleban leaders to try to avert a showdown, U.N. sources said.
Holl made his first trip to Kabul after the Taleban takeover of the city last week, saying he was seeking an early meeting with Dostum as part of efforts to promote national reconciliation.
